newsitem.title: IRAN: The winner is freedom, say jubilant Khatami backers.
newsitem.headline: The winner is freedom, say jubilant Khatami backers.

text.p: Supporters of moderate Shi'ite cleric Mohammad Khatami were jubilant on Saturday after the moderate former culture minister clinched a shock landslide victory over his conservative rival in Iran's presidential election.
"I'm shocked. I really thought it would go to a second round...the winner is freedom," said Behrooz, a 45-year-old housing agent, relaxing with friends.

Iran's Interior Ministry said Khatami, 54, had secured 15.5 million votes by 1430 GMT, nearly three times as many as his closest rival, Parliamentary Speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri, who had been strongly tipped to win but earlier conceded defeat.

The size of the turnout was expected to be the biggest since the country voted to become an Islamic Republic in 1979 and was interpreted by many voters as a clear signal to Tehran's religious elite that the country needed reforms.
Khatami's victory had been helped by his appeal as a moderate and social reformer particularly to Iranian women and the country's large young population, analysts said.

"I am very happy. It was very important that Nateq-Nouri did not become president. For the first time the people have rejected what the establishment wanted," said Mitra, a 20-year- old woman student in a main Tehran shopping street.
More social freedom for young people and for women became a central issue of the campaign together with problems of rampant inflation and unemployment.
Iran's state security apparatus stepped up its profile on key Tehran highways and intersections early as daylight ended.
The government's Guidance Patrol stopped cars to enforce strict Islamic dress codes on drivers and passengers while police and plainclothes security were also evident.
One woman driver wearing a compulsory hejab was rebuked by a female member of the Guidance Patrol outside her car for wearing make-up which is not officially tolerated.
At least one other young woman was put into a white coach with red windows by the patrol. The patrol usually detains violators of dress codes overnight.

"The important thing is that people have voted for someone who attaches importance to civil liberties which have not existed before," said Mori, a 30-year-old man who was listening to a radio in a tailor's shop in central Tehran.
"The government will gradually go towards liberalisation. You can't expect democracy but we hope that people in the future can be more relaxed," he said with a smile.

Some shop owners were handing out boxes of sweet cakes to friends and customers in celebration as news came through on state-run radio that Nateq-Nouri had sent a letter of congratulations to Khatami for his election success.
But post-election celebrations in this city of seven million was muted as many Iranians observed the Shi'ite mourning month of Muharram.
A pro-Khatami clerical group called the Association of Combatant Clerics told supporters not to publicly celebrate because of the religious occasion.
"My heart is thrilled. In my neighbourhood I went to every door asking them to vote for Khatami," said Abolfath, a 65-year-old car park attendant.

"The welfare of the young people will improve, our economy and international relations will also improve...some of the restrictions that existed will be wiped out," said Babak, a 30- year-old computer salesman in the capital.

"People were tired...they wanted a change in their lives... All the young people were active in this election and they wanted social and cultural change," said Ali, a 52-year-old owner of a car radiator factory.

Most voters said that Khatami was committed to solving the country's problems but were also sceptical about how much room for manoeuvre he had while ultimate power remained with the country's supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, backed by an equally arch-conservative Guardian Council and parliament.
"Inflation will come down, opportunities for young people will increase and social restrictions will be eased," said Abolfath, listening intently to his radio in his modest office.
But others thought the task facing Khatami when he replaced President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani would be difficult as he faced strong political and institutional opposition to reform.

"One year from here we will be disillusioned. They filtered the candidates in the first place to make sure they got who they wanted. It was an election between the bad and the worse," said Peyman, a 25-year-old office worker.
Nateq-Nouri's supporters were equally surprised by Khatami's victory and the size of the win.
"I voted for Nateq-Nouri because I thought he was pre- elected before because all the government figures voted for him. I'm just amazed," said Jamshid, a fruit-juice seller.
